summary:
Malapert is a web app for choosing a landing site near the Moon's south pole. There the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° above the horizon, so one hill can cut a lander's
power, and Earth is in view for only about two weeks at a time. Both the site and the landing date matter: on the rim of Shackleton crater, a landing on 15 January 2027 passes
our check, and the same spot a week later fails.

Checking this today takes expert tools. Malapert loads terrain from NASA LOLA data and answers these questions in a few clicks. It has two modes on one calculation engine. The
planning mode has four terrain maps, side-by-side comparison of sites and dates, a site search, an AI assistant and a PDF report. The learning mode gives students a guide
character, short lessons and a landing game that run on the same numbers.

Results were compared with JPL Horizons and NASA illumination maps.
details:
For any point on the terrain and any landing date, Malapert works out when the Sun and Earth are above the local skyline, how steep the ground is, and whether an example

lander's battery lasts the mission. The skyline comes from NASA LOLA elevation data, and Sun and Earth positions come from the Astronomy Engine library. From that the app draws

four maps (terrain, sunlight now, average sunlight, slope), compares two sites or two dates side by side with a GO or NO-GO, searches the region for the best sites against your

criteria, and exports a PDF report. An AI assistant can run the same steps from a written mission description, and it only quotes numbers the app computed.

Mission planners and lander companies get a quick first check of a site and date before paying for a detailed study. Teachers and science centres get a learning mode: students

place a lander, a guide character reacts to the result, and a timed landing game tips the lander over on slopes above 10°, as happened to the IM-1 lander in 2024.

The creative part is that the learning mode runs on the same calculation engine as the planning mode, so a student's lander fails for the same reasons a real one would: terrain

blocks the Sun, or the slope is too steep.

We built it with TypeScript, Next.js, React, three.js (React Three Fiber), Zustand, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, jsPDF, the Anthropic Claude API and Bun, hosted on Cloudflare

Workers.

We put accuracy first and compared our results with JPL Horizons and NASA illumination maps. Screening limits follow NASA landing-site criteria.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA Polar Gridded Digital Elevation Models (PDS)
LOLA average Sun and Earth visibility maps (Mazarico et al. 2011, PGDA)
Glaser et al. 2018, Illumination conditions at the lunar south pole (NTRS)
NASA SVS 4944: Earth and Sun from the Moon's South Pole
projectRefs: Paige et al. 2010, Diviner observations of lunar south-polar cold traps (Science)
Earth observations from the Moon's surface: dependence on libration (AMT 2023)
Inferno colour map polynomial fit (Matt Zucker, Shadertoy)
